reviews.review:
Mahjong Pretty Girls Battle: School Girls Edition is a straightforward take on Japanese mahjong that combines traditional tile-based strategy with a colorful anime presentation. Developed and published by Zoo Corporation, it is clearly designed for players who already enjoy mahjong or want a relatively uncomplicated way to practice it against computer opponents. Instead of transforming the tabletop game into something dramatically different, it keeps the established rules at the center while using its large cast of school-themed characters to provide personality and visual variety.

The actual mahjong implementation is the strongest part of the package. Matches follow authentic Japanese Riichi mahjong rules, requiring players to build valid hands, understand scoring combinations, manage discards, watch opponents' tiles, and judge when taking a risk is worthwhile. Several rule settings and local variations can also be adjusted, giving experienced players some control over how matches operate. Beginners can potentially use it as a practice environment, although the game is more enjoyable when the player already understands at least the fundamentals of Japanese mahjong because it is not built around an extensive teaching campaign.

Its most distinctive feature is the roster of 23 anime-style characters. Every character has her own visual design and Japanese voice acting, with reactions accompanying victories and defeats. This gives otherwise traditional matches a livelier atmosphere and helps distinguish the game from more clinical mahjong simulators. Despite the suggestive presentation, the game does not feature an undressing system or actual nudity during gameplay. The character component is largely cosmetic, serving as a colorful theme wrapped around a conventional mahjong system rather than changing how the game itself works.

One important limitation is that the experience is entirely focused on single-player competition against AI-controlled opponents. This makes it convenient for practicing whenever desired because there is no need to search for human players or depend on active servers. At the same time, the lack of multiplayer significantly reduces its long-term competitive appeal. Mahjong can become particularly compelling when players attempt to read and deceive real opponents, and computer-controlled rivals cannot fully reproduce that psychological element. Consequently, repetition can become noticeable after extended play.

The game should also be viewed as an alternate character edition rather than a completely new sequel. Its core mechanics come from the earlier Mahjong Pretty Girls Battle, with the school-themed character lineup providing the primary change. Anyone who already owns or has spent considerable time with the original should therefore expect familiarity rather than major mechanical innovation. For a newcomer, however, this is less of an issue because the underlying mahjong system remains perfectly capable of delivering satisfying matches.

Visually, the game has a distinctly mid-2010s presentation. The anime artwork remains colorful and expressive, but menus, interfaces, effects, and the overall production feel comparatively modest beside newer digital tabletop games. The Japanese voice performances contribute considerably more personality, particularly because all 23 characters receive voiced reactions. English interface support makes the mechanics more approachable for international players, while Japanese audio preserves the intended character presentation.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable rather than fully Verified. The game runs on SteamOS, its interface text is readable, its normal graphics configuration performs adequately, and the game's functions are accessible with the default controller configuration. There are nevertheless some compromises. Players may encounter non-Steam-Deck button or input icons, and the native display resolution may need to be configured manually. These issues prevent a completely seamless handheld experience, but they are relatively minor for a turn-based mahjong title. Once configured properly, its slower pace makes it naturally suitable for portable sessions.

Ultimately, this is a specialized casual mahjong game whose value depends heavily on what the player expects. Those wanting deep multiplayer competition, elaborate progression, a story campaign, or a modern audiovisual spectacle will find it rather limited. Players interested in authentic Japanese mahjong, AI practice, anime character artwork, and Japanese voice acting have more reason to appreciate it. The 23-character selection gives the package personality, while configurable rules provide enough flexibility to make repeated matches useful for enthusiasts.

As a complete game, it succeeds at delivering functional and enjoyable Japanese mahjong but does relatively little beyond that foundation. Its appealing character designs and voice work make the experience more entertaining, yet the absence of multiplayer and limited advancement over the original prevent it from becoming a particularly substantial mahjong package. It is best approached as a lightweight anime-themed Riichi mahjong game for solo play rather than an all-encompassing digital version of the traditional game.

Rating: 6/10
